title: Heterostructured Photocatalysts for Coupled Organic Pollutant Degradation and Hydrogen Production: From Charge Transfer to Practical Wastewater Reforming
content: The integration of wastewater decontamination with solar hydrogen production represents an emerging strategy for converting environmental remediation into a resource-oriented process. In conventional photocatalytic studies, organic pollutant degradation and hydrogen evolution are often investigated separately, although both processes are governed by the same fundamental requirements: efficient light absorption, charge separation, interfacial redox reactions, and long-term catalyst stability. Heterostructured photocatalysts offer a particularly attractive platform for coupling these reactions, as their engineered interfaces can promote directional charge transfer, suppress electron–hole recombination, and enhance both pollutant oxidation and proton reduction. This review focuses on recent advances in heterostructured photocatalytic materials for simultaneous organic pollutant degradation and hydrogen production, with emphasis on TiO₂-, g-C₃N₄-, MoS₂-, transition-metal-sulfide-, MXene-, MOF-, LDH-, and bismuth-based systems. Special attention is given to type-II, Z-scheme, and S-scheme heterojunctions, as well as defect engineering, oxygen vacancies, noble-metal-free cocatalysts, and interfacial electronic modulation. The mechanistic relationship between charge-transfer pathways, reactive oxygen species formation, pollutant oxidation, and hydrogen evolution is critically discussed. In addition, the role of organic pollutants as oxidizable substrates or electron donors in photocatalytic wastewater reforming is examined. Key performance indicators, including hydrogen evolution rate, apparent quantum efficiency, pollutant removal, mineralization, catalyst stability, reusability, and operation in real wastewater matrices, are analyzed to highlight current limitations in data comparability and practical assessment. Finally, the main challenges associated with long-term stability, mechanistic validation, standardized reporting, catalyst recovery, reactor configuration, and scale-up are discussed. By connecting materials design with environmental photocatalysis and solar fuel generation, this review aims to provide a focused framework for the development of heterostructured photocatalysts capable of transforming polluted water into a platform for clean hydrogen production.
